Senses.Explanation: The headword names a preface: prose placed before a record, collection, or scripture to introduce its compilation, transmission, author, or publication. In the stored evidence, six occurrences are the source's own preface headings, while Yunqi Zhuhong and Hanyue Fazang utter the word when describing requests to preface works. The title blocks also name writers such as Xu Fu, Xiong Kaiyuan, and Yang Yi, but a writer named beside a title is not thereby the utterer of the title's headword.

Entries.SourceTerm: 熏風自南來，殿角生微涼

Senses.PreferredTarget: A warm wind comes from the south; a slight coolness arises by the hall's corner.
SearchAliases: A warm wind comes from the south; a slight coolness arises by the hall's corner.
Senses.Note: All eight distinct current J treatments are retained. Guting quotes Zhongji Neng, while Lianyue, Gulin, Tianran and Zuliang cite Yuanwu; Shiqi, Wenmu and Linwo voice it directly. Linwo's split replies and reunited sermon couplet occur within one occasion and count as one setting. These are separate deployments of shared language, not eight independent coinages or proof that every occurrence was historically spoken by Yuanwu.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB163.xml). Guting Shanjian quotes source-named Zhongji Neng contrasting the endless sky with a single morning's wind and moon; the selected couplet illustrates that immediate occasion, with a warning against accepting either understanding or nonunderstanding. Guting asks what temple objects preach and where implements listen, then says Zhongji has lost his nostrils and he himself drags his tongue. His appended verse rejects idle theorizing. Zhongji is kept unlinked because the short source name does not establish a roster identity.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB183.xml). At the Duan festival hall sermon, Shiqi Tongyun describes rain wetting the ground after prolonged clear weather and immediately taking up the matter, even writing a great auspicious sign across space. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB235.xml). At an early-summer sermon, Lianyue Daozheng places Yuanwu's couplet beside Yunmen's east mountain walking on water, both answers to where Buddhas emerge. He grants the two elders their responsiveness but says they see the sharp point without the square chisel head. Asked today, he would say the whole realm has never hidden it. His replacement answers the cited teachers rather than simply adopting their words as a seasonal description.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB346.xml). Gulin Jiru quotes Foguo Yuanwu raising Yunmen's water-walking answer and replacing it with the wind-and-coolness couplet. While the scriptures are aired, Linwo Jian answers a monk's question about what the assembly should discuss with the south-wind half, then answers the question about a fallen tree's vanished words with the hall-corner coolness half. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB235.xml). At an early-summer sermon, Lianyue Daozheng places Yuanwu's couplet beside Yunmen's east mountain walking on water, both answers to where Buddhas emerge. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB406.xml). Tianran Hanshi cites Dahui's relief on hearing Yuanwu's couplet, then stresses that Yuanwu still held him back as sitting in bare purity and directed him to the further case of words and no words. This teaching contrasts being stopped everywhere with passing one place so that all places open. The phrase is Yuanwu's quoted word in the breakthrough account, while Hanshi uses its insufficiency at that stage to test present assumptions of completion.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB422.xml). While the scriptures are aired, Linwo Jian answers a monk's question about what the assembly should discuss with the south-wind half, then answers the question about a fallen tree's vanished words with the hall-corner coolness half. After blows and a shout, he reunites the couplet in his sermon beside farmers laboring in heat. The single occasion uses the halves responsively and then tests their unity, rather than presenting two independent historical quotations.

Senses.Explanation: A seasonal couplet used as a responsive word in varied teachings. Some records cite it as Yuanwu's answer about where Buddhas emerge; others directly redeploy it for a festival, discerning the master in worldly bustle or an exchange during airing the scriptures. Its function follows each present question, not a single fixed allegory of wind and coolness. Guting Shanjian quotes source-named Zhongji Neng contrasting the endless sky with a single morning's wind and moon; the selected couplet illustrates that immediate occasion, with a warning against accepting either understanding or nonunderstanding. Guting asks what temple objects preach and where implements listen, then says Zhongji has lost his nostrils and he himself drags his tongue. His appended verse rejects idle theorizing. Zhongji is kept unlinked because the short source name does not establish a roster identity. At the Duan festival hall sermon, Shiqi Tongyun describes rain wetting the ground after prolonged clear weather and immediately taking up the matter, even writing a great auspicious sign across space. Asked for a word responsive to season and occasion, he gives the wind-and-coolness couplet. The seasonal scene is the direct setting of his answer, not a new retelling of Yuanwu's interview. At an early-summer sermon, Lianyue Daozheng places Yuanwu's couplet beside Yunmen's east mountain walking on water, both answers to where Buddhas emerge. He grants the two elders their responsiveness but says they see the sharp point without the square chisel head. Asked today, he would say the whole realm has never hidden it. His replacement answers the cited teachers rather than simply adopting their words as a seasonal description.
